newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
MAXIS EXPECTED FOR SYDNEY-TO-HOBART

This year's Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart race is already shaping as a major contest for line honours with suggestions the winning maxis of the past two races, Sayonara (1995) and Morning Glory (1996), will be racing head-to-head for Hobart on Boxing Day.
The two maxis are expected to race in the Admiral's Cup Fastnet Race in August and then be sent Down Under for the ultimate ocean racing clash in the Hobart race.
They are owned by the heads of rival software corporations -- Sayonara by American LARRY ELLISON, who heads Oracle, and Morning Glory by Germany's HASSO PLATTNER, the founder of SAP.
We may also see one or two other overseas maxis and, of course, Sydney yachtsman GEORGE SNOW will be back in action with his re-rigged Brindabella.
There's also overseas interest in the Telstra Southern Cross Cup, the biennial teams series leading up to and including the Hobart race, with teams likely from Europe and Hong Kong.
The Hong Kong team will be headed by Sydney-based Exile, owned by Guess watches manufacturer WARWICK MILLER, with the yacht still on the register of the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club.
Other boats in the team will include two new boats, a BRUCE FARR-designed Cookson-50 and an IAIN MURRAY-designed Sydney-46.
BOOST FOR NEW OLYMPIC CLASS

The Sydney 2000 Olympics yachting programme and the new Australian-designed 49er class were given a major boost with this week's announcement that the Seven television network will cover the SuperSailing circuit for this high-performance skiff.
Seven will broadcast up to 19 hours of sailing in the 1997-98 season with regattas to be held in Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide and Auckland.
To make the events more appealing for viewers, the televised regattas will combine the strict one-design Olympics rules with a less structured format designed purely for spectators.

Speaking at the launch at Royal Sydney Yacht Squadron, ALAN BATEMAN, Seven's Sydney managing director and network director of sport and production, said Seven planned to make sailing a major television sport over the next three years.
BATEMAN said Seven, together with SuperSailing, would introduce technological and production techniques to give sailing a much broader appeal.
SuperSailing will provide up to 25 skiffs for the regatta circuit, which is expected to attract top sailors from overseas as well as the best of local skiff competitors.
The first local to sign up this week was CHRIS NICHOLSON, a two-time world champion in the 505 dinghy class and in 18-footers.

As with the 18-footers, the 49ers competing in SuperSailing will carry advertising on the boats, crews and sails. NICHOLSON will skipper Schneider, a world leader in manufacture and supply for the electrical industry.

SuperSailing is the concept of prominent yachting journalist ROB MUNDLE, television producer PETER SUTTON, managing director of independent television production company Showboat, and RICHARD FRIEDRICHS, owner of Polymedia, which specialises in event management, product launches, exhibitions and 3D media.
PIRATES LOOSE ON PITTWATER
If you happen to be sailing on Pittwater this Sunday make sure you have some pieces of eight (or similar currency) on hand to pay off boarding pirates.

Sunday marks the annual Blackmores Three Island Charity Fun Race to raise money for the Leo & Jenny Leukaemia and Cancer Foundation, which harbour sailors supported in March with the annual Sail for Cancer day.

The Three Islands Race is expected to attract a fleet of nearly 100 yachts sailing out of the Royal Prince Alfred Yacht Club (RPAYC), among them the event sponsor and enthusiastic sailor, MARCUS BLACKMORE.
BLACKMORE, along with organisers ROB MUNDLE (busy week for him) and DAVID STEWART, are confident they can raise A$100,000 from the race itself and a pre-race dinner tonight at the RPAYC.

The race is fun from start to finish, beginning on the club lawns at 10 a.m. with the traditional nip of rum and Le Mans start for skippers to board their yachts and sail the course around Scotland Island on Pittwater, Lion Island in Broken Bay and Dangar Island up the Hawkesbury River.
The "pirates" will be lurking around to help swell the funds as they board unsuspecting boats out for a quieter sail.
MILLENNIUM IN SOLOMONS RACE RECORD

As we reported last week, Coffs Harbour yacht Millennium, skippered by JOHN CLAYTON, established a good lead in the 1,200-nautical mile Solomon Airways race from Brisbane to Gizo in the Solomon Islands.
She held that lead to the finish, slashing 12 hours off the record in finishing more than three hours ahead of Alstar, sailed by the remarkable Lake Macquarie veteran, 82-year-old ALBY BURGIN.
The fleet finished in squally tradewinds and rough seas, Millennium blowing out several spinnakers and bending its spinnaker pole as the crew pushed her hard to maintain the lead to the line.
RSYS HONOURS BRUCE DICKSON

The Royal Sydney Yacht Squadron honoured one of its past commodores, BRUCE DICKSON, by naming him winner of the Idris Trophy for Yachtsman of the Year at this week's prizegiving at the Kirribilli clubhouse.

DICKSON, a member of 40 years, has been a tireless worker for yachting as well as a regular competitor, having served on almost every club committee and the Yachting Association of NSW, of which he is a past president.
More recently he stood in for six months as voluntary chief executive of the Australian Yachting Federation (AYF) to oversee a major restructuring of the national sailing body.
He is now AYF president and is continuing his efforts to raise the status of sailing in Australia.

More than 250 members and their crews attended the prize-giving to collect a glittering array of perpetual trophies and season prizes won in harbour and offshore events conducted by the Squadron over the past season.

Three notable performances were those of GEOFF LEE with his WARWICK HOOD-designed flyer, Styx, in No 1 Division, NEVILLE WITTEY with Yandoo XX in the Etchells one-design class and CARL RYVES with Jennifer in the Dragon class.

LEE and Styx dominated No 1 Division, winning the Boomerang Cup for the main season pointscore as well as taking out the Spring pointscore and finishing second in the Summer series and third in the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia series.

WITTEY scored a remarkable nine first places in the Etchells class, taking out the Xarifa Chalice for the main series as well as winning the spring series, the John "Choco" Winning Memorial Plate and the Kopsen Cup.
WITTEY's wins didn't stop there -- he returned to the Yngling class to take out the Australian championship with Sirocco.

RYVES, a former Olympic sailor, had an even better score -- 10 firsts, five seconds and three thirds to win the main season, spring and summer pointscore with Jennifer, as well as getting his name engraved on a string of perpetual trophies, including the Dragon Gold Cup.
SAFETY AT SEA SEMINAR ON SUNDAY

If you are interested in hearing the inside story of the RAAF's vital role in the search and rescue operation for those upturned yachts in the Vendee Globe race earlier this year, you should contact the Australian Maritime Museum today.
The Safety at Sea Seminar is being held at the museum on Sunday and will also offer the latest information on marine communications and safety.

It includes speakers from the RAAF, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority and Telstra, along with another great survivor, JOHN QUINN, sea safety expert ALISTAIR MITCHELL and JOHN HORNBY, chairman of the Yachting Association's safety committee.
As editor of Offshore Yachting magazine, I'll be chairman of the safety forum at the seminar.
Late bookings can be made with John Wade on 02 9552-7532.
*Peter Campbell is editor of Offshore Yachting magazine.
